title: The Red and the Black
author: Stendhal
description: Julien Sorel, a poor carpenter's son, uses his intelligence and ambition to rise in French society, between love and danger.

paragraphs.t: This is the complete story of The Red and the Black (in French, Le Rouge et le Noir) by Stendhal, published in 1830, retold in English at level B1. The original has two books and seventy-five chapters. Here they are grouped into 20 parts. Every important event of the story is included.

The story takes place in France between about 1826 and 1831. Napoleon has lost his last battle and died, and the old kings are back on the throne. For a poor young man, there are only two ways to rise in the world: the army (the red uniform of the soldier) and the Church (the black robe of the priest). That is one way to understand the title.
Tap any word to see its meaning. Tap a marked phrase to see a grammar note.
The main characters
Julien Sorel — the son of a poor carpenter; intelligent, proud and ambitious
Monsieur de Rênal — the mayor of the small town of Verrières; rich and vain
Madame de Rênal — his wife; gentle, beautiful and innocent
Father Chélan — the old, honest priest of Verrières
Monsieur Valenod — director of the poor-house; Monsieur de Rênal's rival
Fouqué — Julien's only friend, a timber merchant
Father Pirard — the strict director of the seminary in Besançon
The Marquis de La Mole — a powerful nobleman in Paris
Mathilde de La Mole — his daughter; proud, clever and romantic
Count Norbert — Mathilde's brother

The little town of Verrières is one of the prettiest in the region of Franche-Comté, in the east of France. Its white houses, with their pointed roofs of red tiles, lie along the side of a hill. Below the town, the river Doubs runs through a valley. Above it rise the high peaks of the Jura mountains, which are covered with snow from October until May.

When a traveller arrives in Verrières, the first thing he hears is a terrible noise. It comes from a big factory in the main street. Inside, enormous hammers rise and fall with a crash that shakes the ground, and each hammer makes thousands of nails every day. Pretty young girls from the town put small pieces of iron under the hammers, and the pieces come out as nails.
If the traveller asks, "Who owns this fine factory, which makes so much noise?", he is told at once, in a slow, proud voice: "Oh, it belongs to the mayor."

And if the traveller stops for a moment in the main street, he will probably see a tall man walking past with an important air. His hair is grey, and he is dressed in grey. He wears several medals on his coat. He has a high forehead and a nose like a hawk. At first sight, he looks like a gentleman, and even a pleasant one. But after a while, the traveller notices something unpleasant in his face: a look of self-satisfaction, of narrow pride, and of a man who only thinks about money. This man is the mayor, Monsieur de Rênal.

Monsieur de Rênal is very rich. His big house, with its gardens and its walls, is the finest in the town. In Verrières, the most important thing for a man's reputation is the size of his walls. A man who builds big stone walls around his property is respected by everyone. Monsieur de Rênal had built many. He had also bought, at a very high price, a piece of land from an old carpenter named Sorel, who owned a sawmill by the river. Old Sorel was a clever peasant, and he made the mayor pay six times more than the land was worth.

In Verrières, everybody thinks about one thing: making money. Every action is judged by one question: "Will it bring in money?" The people there are not bad, but they are jealous and narrow-minded, and they are always watching each other. In a small town like this, nobody can do anything without the whole town knowing about it. And there is nothing worse in Verrières than to be talked about.
The Public Walk

Above the river, there is a beautiful public walk, with a long terrace and big old plane trees. It is one of the most beautiful views in France. The mayor had made it larger, and it was called the Cours de la Fidélité — the Walk of Loyalty — to show that the town was loyal to the King. There is a stone on the wall with the mayor's name on it.

One day, the mayor ordered the town gardener to cut the branches of the old trees very short, to make them look neat and round. People who loved the trees were angry. One of them was the old priest of Verrières, Father Chélan.
Father Chélan

Father Chélan was eighty years old, but he was still strong and healthy, and he walked straight like a young man. He was honest and kind, and he had a strong sense of justice. He did not care about money or power.

Some time before, a gentleman from Paris named Monsieur Appert had come to Verrières. He was well known for his visits to prisons, hospitals and poor-houses, to see if the poor people inside were treated well. When he arrived, Father Chélan, who knew him, took him to visit the town prison and the poor-house. This made the important people of the town very angry, because they did not want a stranger from Paris to see what was happening there.

The director of the poor-house was Monsieur Valenod. He was a big, loud, red-faced man, with thick black whiskers. He was becoming richer and richer, and everybody whispered that he was stealing money that was meant for the poor. Valenod was furious about the visit, and so was the mayor. They threatened the old priest. "You could lose your position," they told him.

"I am eighty years old," said Father Chélan calmly. "I have lived here for fifty-six years. I baptized almost all of you. If they take my position away, I will live on my small income. But I will not stop doing what I think is right."
A Tutor for the Children

One fine autumn day, Monsieur de Rênal was walking on the public walk with his wife. She was a tall, beautiful woman of about thirty, with a simple, natural grace. She was not a woman who wanted to be admired. She knew nothing about the world, and she did not want to know. She was happy to spend her time with her three little boys.

As they walked, the mayor said, in an important voice: "I have decided to take young Sorel, the carpenter's son, into our house. He will be the tutor for our boys. He knows Latin very well. Father Chélan says that he is a very serious young man, and that he will become a priest. I will pay him three hundred francs a year, and food and lodging."
His wife was surprised. "Why?" she asked.

"Because of Valenod," said the mayor. "Valenod has just bought two beautiful horses from Normandy. He is getting too proud. But he has no tutor for his children. If I have a tutor for mine, people will see that I am more important than he is. That will put him in his place." Then he added: "And besides, I am sure Valenod wants the young man for himself. I must take him first."

Madame de Rênal said nothing. She was not happy with the idea. She imagined a dirty, rough young priest, badly dressed, who would shout at her children and perhaps even beat them. She loved her boys very much, and she was afraid for them.
But her husband had decided. He went the same afternoon to the sawmill to speak to old Sorel.

Old Sorel was very surprised when the mayor offered to take his son Julien into his house. He could not understand why a rich man would want such a useless boy. But he was a clever peasant, and he did not show his surprise. He only said that he would think about it. As soon as the mayor had gone, he went to the sawmill to find his son.

The sawmill stood beside a small stream that came down from the mountains. The water turned a big wheel, and the wheel moved a great saw up and down, cutting the tree trunks into planks. Julien's two older brothers were there, cutting wood with their axes. They were huge, strong men, like giants.

But Julien was not working. Old Sorel looked everywhere for him. At last he saw him. He was sitting high up on one of the beams of the roof, reading a book, while he should have been watching the saw.

Nothing made old Sorel more angry than this. He could not read himself, and he hated books. He thought they were useless. He jumped up, and with one blow of his hand he knocked the book out of Julien's hands and into the stream. With a second blow on the head, he almost made Julien fall from the beam.
"Lazy dog!" he shouted. "Always reading your cursed books, when you should be watching the saw! Come down, you animal! I want to speak to you."

Julien came down. His eyes were full of tears — not because of the pain, but because he had lost his book. It was his favourite book in the world: the Memorial of Saint Helena, the story of Napoleon's last years, told in his own words.
Julien

Julien was a small, slim young man of eighteen or nineteen. He looked weak, but he was strong and could bear a lot of pain. His face was pale and delicate, and he had big, black eyes. When he was calm, those eyes were thoughtful and full of fire. When he was angry, they showed a terrible hatred. His hair was dark brown, and his forehead was low.

His family despised him. His father and brothers beat him often, because he was weak and did not like physical work, and because he always had his nose in a book. Everybody in the family thought he was useless. Julien hated them in return.

He had learned a lot from two people. The first was an old army surgeon who had served under Napoleon. The old man had taught him Latin and history, and had told him many stories about Napoleon's battles. When the surgeon died, he left Julien his medal of the Legion of Honour and his books.
The second was Father Chélan, who had taught him theology. Julien had learned the whole New Testament in Latin by heart. He could recite any page from beginning to end.

Julien had one great dream. He wanted to rise in the world, like Napoleon, who had been born poor and had become Emperor of France. In Napoleon's time, a poor, brave young man could become a general at thirty by fighting in the army. But Napoleon had gone. Now the priests were the most powerful men in France. They were the ones who became rich and important. A bishop could earn a hundred thousand francs a year — three times more than Napoleon's famous generals. So Julien had decided to become a priest. He did not really believe in God. He only wanted power and success.

He had shown his religious knowledge once in front of everyone. Then one day, at a dinner, he had praised Napoleon, and Father Chélan had been displeased. After that, Julien learned to hide his true thoughts. He kept his love of Napoleon a secret, and he always carried his arm in a sling for two months, as a punishment to himself for his mistake. He became a hypocrite. That is the only way, he thought, for a poor man to succeed.
The Offer
Old Sorel told Julien about the mayor's offer. "Answer me without lying, you book-reader," he said. "How do you know Madame de Rênal? When did you speak to her?"
"I have never spoken to her," said Julien. "I have only seen her in church."
"But you looked at her, you hypocrite!"
"Never! You know that in church I only see God," said Julien, with a holy look.
Old Sorel did not believe him. But he understood that this was a chance to make money. "Go and get ready," he said. "Tomorrow we'll go to see the mayor."

When Julien learned that he would live in the mayor's house, he was not happy at first. He was afraid of one thing: he would have to eat with the servants. "I would rather die," he said to himself. His pride could not bear it.

The next day, old Sorel went to see the mayor alone, and he bargained for a long time. He wanted more money. He wanted to know what his son would eat, and where he would sleep. In the end, the mayor agreed to pay four hundred francs a year, and Julien would eat with the family, not with the servants. He would also be given a new suit of black clothes.

Before he went to the mayor's house, Julien went to the church. He wanted to be alone, to think. The church was dark and empty, and the windows were covered with red curtains for a festival. The red light fell on the floor, and it looked like blood. On a bench, Julien found a piece of newspaper. He read: "Details of the execution and last moments of Louis Jenrel, executed at Besançon on..." The rest was torn. Julien noticed that Jenrel had the same letters as his own name, Sorel. He felt a strange chill. Then he saw the red light on the floor again. "It looks like blood," he thought. Then he laughed at himself, and he left the church.

Madame de Rênal was coming out of the drawing room into the garden, with the lightness and grace that were natural to her when nobody was watching. Near the front door, she saw a young peasant. He was very young, and very pale, and he had been crying. He was wearing a clean white shirt and carried a jacket of purple cloth under his arm.

The boy was so pale and gentle that Madame de Rênal, who was a little romantic, thought at first that it was a young girl in disguise, who had come to ask the mayor for some favour. She felt sorry for the poor creature, who seemed afraid to ring the bell. She went towards him.
Julien, who was looking at the door, did not see her coming. He jumped when a soft voice said, near his ear: "What do you want here, my child?"
He turned round quickly, and he was so struck by her kind, gentle look that he forgot his shyness. He forgot everything, even why he had come. He saw only her beauty. She repeated her question.
"I have come to be the tutor, madame," he said at last, ashamed of his tears, which he tried to wipe away.

Madame de Rênal could not speak. They were very close to each other, looking at each other. Julien had never seen a person so well dressed, especially a woman with such a fine, white complexion, speaking to him so gently. Madame de Rênal looked at the big tears on the young man's cheeks, which had been so pale and were now so pink. Then she began to laugh, with the wild happiness of a young girl. She laughed at herself, and she could not believe her happiness. So this was the tutor she had imagined as a dirty, rough priest who would shout at her children!
"What, sir?" she said at last. "You know Latin?"
The word "sir" surprised Julien so much that he thought for a moment. "Yes, madame," he said shyly.
Madame de Rênal was so happy that she said: "You will not be too hard on my poor boys?"
"I? Hard on them? Why?"
"You will be kind to them, won't you, sir?" she said, more gently. "You promise me?"

To hear himself called "sir" again, seriously, by such a well-dressed lady, was more than Julien had ever hoped. In his dreams of glory, he had always told himself that no fine lady would speak to him until he wore a splendid uniform. Madame de Rênal, for her part, was completely charmed by his beautiful complexion, his big black eyes and his pretty hair, which was curling more than usual because he had put his head in the cold water of the fountain to cool it.
"What is your name, sir?" she asked, in a sweet voice.

"Julien Sorel, madame. I am trembling as I enter a strange house for the first time in my life. I need your protection, and you must forgive me for many things in the first days. I have never been to school; I was too poor. I have only spoken to my cousin, the army surgeon, and to Father Chélan. My brothers always beat me. Don't believe them if they speak badly of me. Forgive my faults, madame. I will never have bad intentions."
Then she led him into the house.
The Latin Test

Monsieur de Rênal came and looked at Julien with a critical eye. He took him to his room and gave him a new black suit. "You must never see your family again," he said. "Their manners are not suitable for my children."

When Julien came back wearing his new black clothes, he looked like a different person — serious and dignified, like a young priest. Monsieur de Rênal brought in the three little boys and introduced them.

"Gentlemen," Julien said to the children, with great seriousness, "I am here to teach you Latin. You know what it is to recite a lesson. Here is the Holy Bible. Open it anywhere, and read me the first three words of a paragraph. I will recite the whole page by heart, until you tell me to stop."

The eldest boy, Adolphe, opened the book and read three words. Julien recited the whole page in Latin, as easily as if he were speaking French. Monsieur de Rênal looked at his wife proudly, as if to say: "You see what a tutor I have found!" The children were amazed. The servants came to the door to listen. Then some friends of the family arrived, and Julien did it again for them. Soon the whole town was talking about the mayor's wonderful tutor.
Life in the House

In less than a month, Julien had won the respect of everyone in the house. The children loved him. He did not love them, but he was patient, fair and serious with them, and he never beat them. He was cold and polite to Monsieur de Rênal, whom he secretly despised. He hated the rich, and he felt that everyone in this house looked down on him because he was poor. When the family laughed at something, Julien thought they were laughing at him.

Madame de Rênal, on the other hand, was very kind to him. She noticed that he had very few clothes. One day, she gave him some money — a few gold coins — and said, "Buy yourself some new shirts. But please don't tell my husband."

Julien's pride was terribly hurt. He went red and stood up very straight. "Madame, I am poor, but I am not a servant," he said coldly. "I cannot accept money from you secretly. It would be lacking in respect towards your husband."

Madame de Rênal was surprised and hurt. She had only wanted to be kind. But she admired him even more for his pride. Instead, she bought the shirts for him with her own money, and paid for books for the children, which Julien could use.
Elisa

Madame de Rênal's maid, Elisa, was a young woman who had just received a small inheritance. She fell in love with Julien and told Father Chélan that she wanted to marry him. Father Chélan called Julien and told him about it. It was a good chance for a poor young man: Elisa had money.
But Julien refused. He did not want to marry a servant. He wanted much more from life. "I want to become a priest," he told Father Chélan.

The old priest looked at him with doubt. "My son," he said, "I am afraid you do not have a true calling to the Church. I see in you a dark fire that does not come from God. Think carefully before you choose."
When Madame de Rênal heard that Julien had refused to marry Elisa, she felt a strange joy. She did not understand why. She was so innocent that she did not yet know she was in love.

chapters.title: Part 4 — A Hand in the Dark

paragraphs.t: In the spring, the family moved to their country house at Vergy, a village in the mountains, about two hours from Verrières. There was an old castle there, with a big garden and a forest of walnut trees, and a beautiful view over the valley of the Doubs.

Madame de Rênal was very happy at Vergy. She ran in the garden with her children and chased butterflies with them, using big nets of thin cloth. Julien, who was free from the eyes of the town, felt happy too. He went for long walks alone in the mountains, and he read his books about Napoleon. In the evenings, everyone sat in the garden under a big lime tree.

Madame de Rênal's cousin, Madame Derville, came to stay with them. She was a clever, sensible woman. She soon noticed that her cousin was different — happier, more lively and more beautiful than before. And she noticed the young tutor. She began to suspect what Madame de Rênal herself did not understand.
Madame de Rênal began to dress more carefully. She asked for new summer dresses to be made. She did not ask herself why.
The Decision
One evening, while they were sitting in the dark garden, Julien's hand touched Madame de Rênal's hand by chance. She quickly pulled her hand away.

Julien felt insulted. "She pulled her hand away from me because I am a poor peasant," he thought. And he decided that the next evening, he would take her hand, and she would leave it in his. It was not love that made him decide this. It was pride. He felt that it was his duty, like a soldier who must win a battle. If he failed, he would despise himself.

All the next day, he thought about it. He was so nervous that he could hardly speak to anyone. He watched the clock. He told himself: "At exactly ten o'clock tonight, I will do what I promised myself, or I will go up to my room and shoot myself."

In the evening, the three of them sat under the lime tree in the dark: Madame de Rênal, Madame Derville and Julien. The night was hot and heavy. A storm was coming. Julien was so nervous that his voice changed, and he could not talk normally. Madame de Rênal noticed and asked him if he was ill.
Every stroke of the church clock sounded in Julien's heart. Nine o'clock. A quarter past nine. Half past nine. A quarter to ten. Julien felt sick with fear. He despised himself for his cowardice.
At last, the clock began to strike ten. With each stroke, Julien felt as if a hammer was hitting his chest. When the last stroke sounded, he put out his hand and took Madame de Rênal's hand.

She tried to pull it away. But he held it firmly. Her hand was cold, and it trembled. Julien pressed it with a strength he did not know he had. She made one more effort to free it, and then she left her hand in his.

Julien's heart was full of joy — not because he loved Madame de Rênal, but because he had won. He had done his duty. He felt like a general after a victory. He began to talk easily and cheerfully, and he talked so well that Madame Derville was amazed.
Madame de Rênal said nothing. She was too moved to speak. She was afraid that if she spoke, Madame Derville would notice something. Her hand stayed in Julien's for the rest of the evening.

When they went to bed, Julien slept like a man after a battle. But Madame de Rênal did not sleep at all. For the first time in her life, she was in love. She was happy, and she was terrified. "Is this what love is?" she thought. "This strange happiness? It is a sin!" She was a good, religious woman. She thought of her husband and her children. She thought she was a terrible woman. And then she thought of Julien's eyes, and she was happy again. She spent the whole night in this storm of feelings.
The next morning, Julien felt only a little proud of his victory. He had almost forgotten it. He went for a walk in the mountains and read his book about Napoleon.
The Portrait
A few days later, Monsieur de Rênal decided to change the mattresses in all the beds in the house. He told the servants to bring all the straw mattresses down, and to put new ones in their place.

Julien was suddenly very pale. "Madame," he whispered to Madame de Rênal, "I have a secret. In my mattress, there is a small box. Inside it is a portrait. If your husband finds it, I am lost. Please, please, go to my room and take it out before anyone sees it. And promise me that you won't look at it."

Madame de Rênal ran upstairs and found the box. She was very pale too. "A portrait!" she thought. "It must be the portrait of a woman — a woman he loves!" She felt terrible jealousy. But she did not open the box. She gave it to Julien, who thanked her and ran into the garden. There, he burned the portrait.
It was not the portrait of a woman. It was a picture of Napoleon. If Monsieur de Rênal, who hated Napoleon and loved the King, had found it, he would have sent Julien away at once.
On the Mountain

Sometimes Julien climbed alone to the top of a high rock above the valley. From there, he could see for many miles. He watched a big hawk flying in great circles in the sky. It moved quietly and powerfully, without effort. Julien envied it. "That was Napoleon's destiny," he thought. "One day, will it be mine?"
Fouqué

After the evening of the hand, Julien asked for a few days of holiday, and he went to visit his only friend, Fouqué. Fouqué was a timber merchant who lived alone in a small house high in the mountains. He was a simple, honest, cheerful man.

Julien climbed for hours through the forest. On the way, he found a small cave high up in the rocks. He sat there alone, looking down at the whole valley, and he felt completely free. He lit a fire and wrote down his thoughts, and then he burned the paper. Nobody must know his secret dreams.

At Fouqué's house, his friend made him an offer. "Julien," he said, "I have a good business, and I am making money. Come and work with me. You are clever, you can write and count. In a few years, you will earn four thousand francs a year. We will be partners."

It was a good offer, and Julien thought about it seriously. It would mean a quiet, safe life, without lies. But it would also mean giving up his great dreams. To be a timber merchant in the mountains, when he wanted to be Napoleon! He refused. Fouqué was disappointed. "You are a strange fellow," he said.
Two O'Clock

When Julien returned to Vergy, Madame de Rênal was so happy to see him that she could not hide it. Julien noticed. He thought: "This woman is in love with me. I must become her lover. It is my duty." Again, it was pride that pushed him, not love. He felt that he had to win her, as Napoleon had to win a battle. And he wanted to take revenge on her husband, and on all the rich people who looked down on him.
One evening, when they were alone, he whispered to her: "Madame, tonight at two o'clock I shall come to your room. I have something to tell you."
She was shocked and angry. "Never!" she said. "How dare you!"

Julien felt humiliated. But he had made a decision, and he would not change it. At two o'clock in the morning, he went along the dark corridor in his bare feet, trembling. His heart was beating so hard that he thought he would faint. He would rather have faced a firing squad. At the door of her room, he stopped. "If I don't go in now, I am a coward," he told himself. He opened the door.
Madame de Rênal jumped out of bed when she saw him. "Go away!" she cried. "You are terrible!"
Julien forgot all his plans, all his careful phrases. He fell on his knees beside her bed, took her hand, and began to cry. He cried like a child. And she, who loved him, could not resist his tears.

A few hours later, when Julien left her room, he was not as happy as he had expected. "Is this all?" he thought. "Is this what it is to be loved?" He was proud of his victory, but he had not felt the great passion he had read about in books. He had been too busy thinking about how to act, like a soldier following his orders.
True Love

But in the days that followed, everything changed. Madame de Rênal loved him with a pure, simple, total love. She did not think about her reputation, or about the danger. She only thought about him. When they were together, she was so happy that she seemed younger, almost like a girl.

Little by little, Julien forgot his pride and his calculations. He was young, and she was beautiful and kind, and she loved him. He began to love her too. In her arms, he forgot his hatred of the rich and his dreams of glory. He felt for the first time that someone cared for him, not for his Latin or his cleverness, but for himself.

She also taught him many things he did not know: how to behave in society, how to speak to important people, what to say and what not to say. Julien was a peasant's son, and he knew nothing about these things. She did it gently, without hurting his pride. She was ten years older than he was, but in some things she was like a child, and he was the one who knew more.

They spent the summer in happiness. When Monsieur de Rênal was away, they walked in the garden for hours. When he was there, they hid their feelings, and Julien was as cold and polite as before. Monsieur de Rênal noticed nothing. He only thought about his money and his rivals.
The Child's Illness
Then one day, the youngest boy, Stanislas, became very ill with a high fever. For several days, the doctors thought he would die.

Madame de Rênal was in despair. And a terrible idea came into her mind: God was punishing her for her sin. She was an adulteress, and now God was going to take her child from her. She sat by the boy's bed day and night, crying and praying. "Oh, God, take me, not him! Punish me, not my innocent child!"

She wanted to tell her husband everything — to confess her sin, so that God would forgive her and save her son. Julien was terrified. If she confessed, she would be ruined, and he would be ruined too.
"If you tell him," he said to her, "he will throw you out. You will lose your children, your home, your reputation. Everyone in Verrières will talk about you. And that will not save Stanislas."
"I don't care about myself," she said. "I only care about my son. I have sinned, and I must pay for it."

Julien saw how much she suffered. For the first time, he did not think about himself. He saw that her love was real — so real that she was ready to destroy herself for it. He felt deep pity and tenderness for her. "If I could," he thought, "I would die for her."

At last, after many terrible days, Stanislas got better. The fever went down, and he began to eat again. Madame de Rênal thanked God on her knees. She did not confess. But from that time, there was always a little shadow of guilt in her happiness. And Julien loved her more than before.

One day, a great piece of news arrived in Verrières: the King was going to visit the region! He would pass through Verrières on his way to pray at the famous church of Bray-le-Haut, where the bones of a holy saint were kept.

The whole town was excited. Everyone wanted to see the King and to be seen by him. The mayor decided that there would be a guard of honour: young men from the best families of the town, on horseback, in beautiful blue uniforms with silver decorations, to ride beside the King's carriage.

Madame de Rênal had an idea. She wanted Julien to be in the guard of honour. She knew how much he would love to wear a uniform and ride a horse like a soldier. She did everything she could to arrange it, and in the end she succeeded. Monsieur de Rênal agreed, because he thought it would show everyone how important his household was.
The other families of Verrières were furious. "What?" they said. "The son of a carpenter, riding with our sons, in front of the King? It is a scandal!" Monsieur Valenod was the most angry of all.
The Uniform

On the great day, Julien wore the blue uniform with silver buttons, and a tall hat with feathers. He rode a beautiful horse that belonged to a rich gentleman. He had never ridden a horse in front of so many people, and at first he was afraid. But he rode well, and he was very handsome in his uniform. The young women of the town looked at him and whispered. Madame de Rênal, standing at a window, watched him with pride and love.

When the King's carriage arrived, the crowd shouted, "Long live the King!" The guard of honour rode beside the carriage. For a few moments, Julien felt like a hero. He was a soldier! He was riding next to a king! "This is how it was with Napoleon's officers," he thought. His heart was full of joy.
But his horse got frightened by the noise of the crowd, and he almost fell off. Everyone laughed. Julien went red, but he stayed in the saddle.
The Church

After the procession, Julien quickly took off his uniform and put on his black clothes again. Father Chélan had asked him to help at the ceremony in the church of Bray-le-Haut, as an assistant to the priests.

The church was very beautiful, decorated with gold and flowers and hundreds of candles. A young bishop, the Bishop of Agde, had come to lead the ceremony. He was only about thirty years old, and he was handsome and elegant. Julien was surprised. "So young," he thought, "and already a bishop! And how much money does he earn?"

Before the ceremony, Julien found the young bishop alone in a room, practising in front of a mirror. He was giving blessings to the empty air with his hand, carefully, again and again, to make sure that his movements looked graceful and noble. Julien watched him, amazed. "This is what power is," he thought. "It is a performance, like the theatre."

During the ceremony, the King knelt in front of the saint's bones, and the bishop gave the blessing. All the people fell on their knees. The music was beautiful. Julien was moved in spite of himself. For a moment, he felt that he could become a priest, and even a bishop, if he played his part well.
But he had seen the bishop practising in front of the mirror, and he could not forget it.
After the Visit

After the King's visit, everybody in Verrières talked about Julien. Some admired him. Many were jealous. People began to say that he was too proud, too ambitious. "Who does he think he is?" they said. "The carpenter's son on a horse, in front of the King!"

Father Chélan was worried. He had heard the rumours, and he was afraid for Julien. "My son," he said, "be careful. You have enemies now. And I am afraid that your heart is not with God. Think about what you really want."
Julien listened politely, but he did not change. He was proud of his success. And he was happy, because Madame de Rênal loved him more than ever.
But in Verrières, everyone watches everyone. And Elisa, the maid whom Julien had refused to marry, was watching him very carefully.

Elisa had seen many things. She had noticed that Julien and Madame de Rênal often walked alone together. She had noticed the looks between them. And she was jealous and angry, because Julien had refused to marry her. So she went to Monsieur Valenod and told him everything she suspected.

Valenod was delighted. He hated the mayor. He also had another reason to hate Madame de Rênal: years before, he had tried to court her, and she had refused him. Now he had a chance for revenge. He wrote a letter without signing it — an anonymous letter — and sent it to Monsieur de Rênal. The letter said that his wife was in love with the young tutor.

When Monsieur de Rênal read the letter, he was very upset. He walked up and down in his room all night. He did not know what to do. Was it true? He did not really believe it. He had never imagined that his wife could love anyone, and especially not a poor peasant. But he could not forget the letter.

He was not jealous like a man in love. He was jealous like a man who is afraid of being laughed at. "If this is true," he thought, "the whole town will laugh at me. I will be ridiculous." Then he thought of other things. If he sent his wife away, he would lose her money. She was going to inherit a large fortune from an old aunt. If he fought Julien in a duel, everyone would know. Either way, he would lose.
A Plan

Madame de Rênal saw that her husband was troubled. She soon found out about the letter. She was frightened, but she was also brave. She loved Julien, and she would do anything to protect him. With a cleverness that surprised Julien, she made a plan.

"We will make a second anonymous letter," she said. "A letter to me this time, that looks like it comes from the same person. Cut out words from a book and stick them on a piece of paper. I will show it to my husband, and I will be very angry. I will say that someone is trying to destroy our family, and I will ask him to send you away. Then he will think it is all a plot by his enemies, and that I am innocent."
Julien made the letter. He cut out words from an old book and stuck them on a page. Madame de Rênal showed it to her husband with tears of anger.

"Look," she said. "Someone has sent this horrible letter to me. It is an insult! I am sure it is Monsieur Valenod. He has always hated you, and he wants to make you look ridiculous. Send the young man away, if you like. But don't let these people think that they can frighten the mayor of Verrières!"

Monsieur de Rênal was confused. His wife was so angry, and she spoke so honestly, that he began to believe her. He decided that the letters were only a trick by his enemies. He did not send Julien away. But he was still uneasy, and the gossip in the town did not stop.
Dinner at Valenod's

During this time, Julien was invited to dinner at Monsieur Valenod's house. Valenod wanted to take him away from the mayor and have him as tutor for his own children. Julien went, because he wanted to see what kind of man Valenod was.

The house was large and full of expensive furniture, all new and in bad taste. The dinner was rich, with fine wines. Valenod was loud and vulgar. He boasted about his money, his horses and his friends in high places. The guests were all rich men who laughed at his jokes.

The poor-house, which Valenod managed, was next door. During the dinner, Julien heard the poor people singing in the next building. Valenod became angry and sent a servant to stop them. "Those beggars are making too much noise," he said.

Julien felt sick. These poor people had nothing, and Valenod was growing rich with the money meant for them. Here he was, eating and drinking in luxury, while they were hungry next door. Julien almost wept. But he hid his feelings and was very polite. He was learning to be a hypocrite.
Father Chélan's Decision
But the rumours about Julien and Madame de Rênal continued to grow. Everyone in Verrières was talking about them. At last, Father Chélan called Julien.

"My son," he said seriously, "I do not want to know what is true and what is not. But for your own good, and for the good of others, you must leave Verrières. You must go to the seminary at Besançon to study for the priesthood. If you do not want to do that, then go to your friend Fouqué and become a merchant. But you cannot stay here."
Julien knew that the old priest was right. He agreed to go to the seminary.
When Madame de Rênal heard the news, she was in despair. But she understood that it was the only way. Monsieur de Rênal, too, was secretly relieved.

On the last night, Julien went to her room. They did not speak much. She was pale and cold, and she held him in silence. She cried, but she did not complain. She seemed to have already said goodbye to life. Julien was surprised and hurt by her coldness. He did not understand that she was trying not to break down completely.
The next morning, he left Verrières. As the carriage went down the road, he looked back at the house. He thought of her, and he felt a great pain in his heart.

From the top of a hill, Julien saw Besançon for the first time. It was a big city, with high walls and strong fortifications, built by the old kings. He thought it was one of the prettiest cities in France. "How I would love to be a soldier here, defending these walls!" he thought.
But he was not going to be a soldier. He was going to be a priest.
The Café

He arrived early in the morning and walked around the city. He was hungry, so he went into a big café. It was the first café he had ever seen, and it seemed very grand to him: there were big mirrors, marble tables and men playing billiards. The men looked at him and laughed at his country clothes.

At the counter sat a young woman. She was the cashier. She was pretty, with bright eyes and a kind smile. Julien was shy, but he spoke to her. He told her that he was going to the seminary. Her name was Amanda Binet. She was kind to him and gave him a cup of coffee and some bread.
"You're very young to become a priest," she said, looking at him with interest. "And very handsome."

They talked for a few minutes, while she was not busy. She told him that if he ever came back to the café, he could say that he was her cousin. She gave him her address. Then a big young man came in, who seemed to be her lover. He looked at Julien angrily, and Julien wanted to fight him. But Amanda begged him not to, and he left.
The Seminary

The seminary was a big, gloomy building near the cathedral. Over the door there was an iron cross. Julien rang the bell. After ten minutes, a pale man in black opened the door, looked at him without speaking, and led him through long, dark corridors to a small room.

There, behind a desk covered with papers, sat a man in an old black robe. He was very thin, with a face so pale and hard that it seemed to be made of stone. He did not look up for a long time. This was Father Pirard, the director of the seminary.

Julien was so frightened that he almost fainted. His legs were shaking. He had never felt such fear, not even when his father beat him. At last, Father Pirard looked up. His eyes were small and black and very sharp, like the eyes of a hunter.
"Come here," he said. "What is your name?"
"Julien Sorel, Father."

Father Pirard read the letter of recommendation from Father Chélan. Then he asked Julien questions in Latin about the Bible and about theology. Julien answered perfectly. Father Pirard was surprised. He asked more difficult questions. Julien answered them too. Then Father Pirard asked him about the Church Fathers — the great writers of the early Church. Julien knew them all.

At last, Father Pirard said: "Your answers are good. You have a good memory. But I see that you are proud. Pride is a great sin, my son. Here, you must learn to be humble. You will obey all the rules. You will not leave the seminary without my permission. You will not receive any letters without my reading them first. And you will have no friends. Do you understand?"
"Yes, Father."

"Father Chélan writes that you have no money. I will give you a scholarship. You will not pay anything. But I warn you: here, there are many who will hate you, because you are clever and because you are not like them. Be careful."

Then he called a servant, and Julien was taken to a small, cold cell on the top floor. There was a bed, a chair and a small window. From the window he could see the walls of the city, and beyond them the green hills and the river.

When he was alone, Julien sat on the bed and thought: "Here, I must be a hypocrite every minute of every day. Here, I must hide everything that I am. This is my battlefield. Napoleon fought with guns. I will fight with lies."
He did not know how hard it would be.

Life in the seminary was hard. Every day was the same. The students got up at five o'clock in the morning, prayed, went to classes, prayed again, ate in silence, and went to bed at nine. They wore long black robes, and they walked with their eyes on the ground. There were about three hundred of them.

Julien had expected to meet clever, serious young men, who loved learning and God. He was disappointed. Most of the students were sons of poor peasants, like himself. But they did not want to become priests because they loved God. They wanted to become priests because a priest always has enough to eat. For them, the Church was a way to escape from hard work in the fields. They were ignorant and lazy, and they were very good at one thing: pretending to be holy.

Julien soon found that his intelligence was a danger here. When he answered questions well in class, the other students hated him. When he read books, they said he was proud. They called him "Martin Luther", after the great heretic, because he thought too much. Nobody here wanted a student who thought. The ideal student was one who obeyed, prayed and believed without asking questions.
Learning to Pretend

So Julien decided to change. He studied the other students carefully, as an actor studies a role. He noticed how they walked, how they held their heads, how they lowered their eyes. He noticed that the most respected students were those who ate their food with the most humility, and who looked at the crucifix with the most devotion.

He practised walking like them. He practised looking stupid. He even practised the way they ate their eggs at breakfast. But it was very difficult. He could not hide the fire in his eyes. After many months, he was still not good at it.

One day, while he was eating, he looked up at the window and saw a beautiful blue sky. His face showed his joy for a moment. A teacher saw him. "Sorel," he said, "you look at the sky like a pagan. A true Christian thinks of heaven, not of the sky."

Everyone watched him. There were spies everywhere. One of the teachers, Father Castanède, was the chief of the spies. He encouraged the students to report everything they saw. He wanted to destroy Father Pirard, whom he hated, and he knew that Julien was Father Pirard's favourite.
Julien received no letters. Madame de Rênal wrote to him, but her letters were stopped. He did not know if she had forgotten him.
Father Pirard

Father Pirard was the only person who understood Julien. He was a strict man, but honest. He belonged to a group of priests called Jansenists, who believed in a pure and strict religion. He hated the hypocrisy and the politics of the Church, and he had many enemies.

He watched Julien carefully. One day, he called him to his room and gave him a job: he would be the tutor for the New and Old Testament for the other students. It was a great honour. The other students hated Julien even more.

Then the examinations came. Julien was the best student in the seminary. But in the oral examination, a priest asked him a trick question about a pagan writer, Horace. Julien, who loved Horace, answered with enthusiasm and quoted many lines. The examiners smiled and wrote down that Julien knew pagan writers better than the Bible. They gave him a low mark — the 198th place out of all the students! It was an injustice, done to hurt Father Pirard.
Corpus Christi

On the festival of Corpus Christi, Julien was sent to help decorate the cathedral of Besançon. He worked high up on a ladder, hanging red silk curtains on the great columns. He was brave and skilful, and the old priest in charge of the cathedral was delighted with him.
During the ceremony, Julien was alone near a chapel of the cathedral. He saw two ladies kneeling at a prayer stool. One of them turned her head. It was Madame de Rênal!
When she saw him, she gave a little cry and fainted. The other lady, who was Madame Derville, held her up. "Go away, sir!" she said angrily to Julien. "Don't come near her!"

Julien could not move. He stood there, white and trembling, until the two ladies had gone. All day long, he could think of nothing else. "She is still alive. She is in Besançon. She saw me, and she fainted. She still loves me!" But he did not try to see her again.
The Offer

Father Pirard's enemies were growing stronger. In the end, he was forced to resign from the seminary. But he had a powerful friend in Paris: the Marquis de La Mole, one of the richest noblemen in France. Father Pirard had helped him for many years in an important lawsuit against another powerful man. Now the Marquis offered him a position as priest of a parish near Paris.
Before he left, Father Pirard called Julien to his room.

"My son," he said, "I am leaving Besançon. And I am afraid that, without me, my enemies will destroy you. The Marquis de La Mole needs a secretary. I have recommended you. You will live in his house in Paris. He will pay you one hundred louis a year. Do you accept?"
Julien could not believe it. Paris! The great capital, the centre of the world! And a powerful marquis, a man of the highest nobility! It was more than he had ever hoped for.
"Yes, Father," he said. "With all my heart."

Father Pirard looked at him sadly. "Be careful in Paris, my son," he said. "It is a dangerous city for a young man like you. And remember: you have only your talent. The people you will meet will have everything else."
On his way to Paris, Julien could not resist. He went back to Verrières to see Madame de Rênal one last time. It had been fourteen months since he had left.

He arrived at night and walked to the house. Everything was dark. He found a long ladder in the garden, which the gardener used for the fruit trees. He carried it to the wall under her window and climbed up. His heart was beating fast. He knocked very softly on the window.
For a long time, nothing happened. Then the window opened a little. Madame de Rênal looked out. When she saw him, she was terrified.
"Go away!" she whispered. "Go away at once! I have repented. God has forgiven me. I will never see you again."

During the fourteen months, she had suffered terribly. She had believed that her love was a great sin, and she had confessed it to a priest. She had prayed and fasted, and she had promised God that she would never see Julien again. She had tried to forget him. She had become very religious.

But Julien did not go away. He climbed into the room. He talked to her for a long time in the dark. He told her about the seminary, about his loneliness, about his suffering. She listened in silence. Then he told her that he was going to Paris, and that he would probably never see her again. She began to cry.
At last, in spite of all her promises, she could not resist him. She threw herself into his arms. All her religious fears disappeared in a moment of happiness. She loved him more than ever.
Hidden in the Room

When the morning came, Julien could not leave. There were servants everywhere in the garden. Madame de Rênal hid him in her room all day. She brought him food that she had taken secretly from the kitchen, and they laughed like children at the danger. She was so happy that she forgot everything.
In the afternoon, her husband came to her door and knocked. "Open the door! I want to speak to you!"

Madame de Rênal hid Julien under a pile of clothes in a corner of the room. Then she opened the door. Her husband came in and talked about some business. He walked around the room. Julien, under the clothes, held his breath. Monsieur de Rênal did not see anything. At last he left.
The Escape
That night, Julien prepared to leave. But just as he was climbing down the ladder, a servant saw him in the moonlight and gave the alarm.
"Thieves! Thieves!" he shouted.
Julien jumped down and ran across the garden. Shots were fired behind him. A bullet passed close to his head. He ran faster, climbed over the wall, and escaped into the night.
When he was far away, and safe, he stopped to catch his breath. He looked back at the dark house. He knew he would never see her again. "Goodbye," he whispered. Then he took the road to Paris.
Behind him, Madame de Rênal stood at her window, trembling. She had heard the shots. She did not know if he was alive or dead.
Here ends the first book of the story.

When Julien arrived in Paris, the first thing he did was visit the places connected with Napoleon. He went to Malmaison, the house where the Emperor had lived with Josephine, and he cried there. Then he went to see Father Pirard, who took him to the house of the Marquis de La Mole.

The Hôtel de La Mole was a huge, magnificent building in the rich Faubourg Saint-Germain, where the oldest noble families of France lived. There was a big courtyard, a garden, and many beautiful rooms with gold, mirrors and silk. Julien had never seen anything like it. He felt very small.

"Be careful," whispered Father Pirard as they went up the great staircase. "Here, the slightest mistake will be noticed. They will judge you by your manners, not by your intelligence. Don't show your feelings. And don't be proud."
The Marquis

The Marquis de La Mole was a small, thin man with lively eyes and a grey wig. Julien had expected a proud, cold nobleman. Instead, he found a polite, elegant man who spoke to him kindly. The Marquis looked at him carefully and said a few words. Then he said to Father Pirard, in a low voice, "He seems intelligent. Let's see how he writes."

He gave Julien a letter to copy. When Julien finished, the Marquis looked at it and smiled. "You have written cela with two l's," he said. "That is a mistake. Be careful with your spelling." Julien went red with shame. He would never forget that small mistake.

The Marquis gave him a room in the house, an office in the library, and a salary. He also gave him money to buy fine clothes, and he sent a tailor, a dancing master and a fencing master to teach him. "You must look like a gentleman," he said. "In Paris, appearance is everything."

Julien worked very hard. He spent all day in the library, writing letters, copying documents and organising the Marquis's papers. He was intelligent and careful, and the Marquis was soon very pleased with him. Within a few months, Julien was managing many of the Marquis's business affairs.
The Family
At dinner, Julien met the rest of the family.
The Marquise de La Mole was a tall, cold, proud woman. She only cared about noble birth. For her, a man who was not of noble family did not exist. She hardly looked at Julien.
Their son, Count Norbert, was a handsome, elegant young man, polite and kind but a little empty. He was always busy with his horses and his friends.

And there was their daughter, Mathilde. She was nineteen years old, tall and slim, with beautiful blonde hair and very bright blue eyes. She was very beautiful, but there was something cold and proud in her face. Julien did not like her at first. "She has the eyes of a cat," he thought. "She is too proud. She looks at me as if I were a piece of furniture."
Mistakes

In the first weeks, Julien made many mistakes. He did not know how to behave in a rich Paris house. Once, he rode a horse in the street and fell off in front of everybody. Count Norbert laughed, but kindly. "You ride like a priest," he said. Another time, Julien got into an argument with a man in a café, and challenged him to a duel. He fought and was slightly wounded. Later, he found out that the man was only a servant who had stolen his master's name.

Julien was very ashamed of these mistakes. But the Marquis was amused by them. He liked Julien's energy and his originality. "He is different from the young men of our class," he said to Father Pirard. "They are all the same. They have no fire. This young man is like a volcano."

The Marquis became fond of him. When he was ill with gout and had to stay in bed, he asked Julien to sit with him and talk. They talked about everything: history, politics, books, Napoleon. The Marquis was surprised by Julien's intelligence.

One day, the Marquis said: "My dear Sorel, I want to give you a present. Here is a blue coat. When you wear the blue coat, you will be my friend, and we will talk as equals. When you wear your black coat, you will be my secretary, and I will give you orders." Julien was deeply moved by this kindness.
The Salon

Every evening, many important people came to the Marquise's drawing room — dukes, generals, ambassadors, bishops and rich bankers. Julien sat in a corner and watched them. He was disappointed. They were rich and elegant, but they were terribly boring. They never talked about anything important. They were afraid of ideas, afraid of anything new, afraid of the future. They only talked about the weather, about horses, about who had married whom. Nobody said anything clever, because it was dangerous to be clever.
"So this is high society," Julien thought. "These are the masters of France. They are not better than the people of Verrières. They are only more polite."

Mathilde de La Mole was the most admired young woman in Paris. She was beautiful, rich and of the highest nobility. Many young noblemen wanted to marry her, and one of them, the Marquis de Croisenois, was almost certainly going to be her husband. He was rich, handsome, polite and very boring.

Mathilde was bored too. She was bored by everything: the balls, the parties, the compliments, the young men who were all exactly the same. She was very intelligent, and she read many books — including books that a young lady was not supposed to read. She despised the people around her. She felt that she had been born in the wrong century.
The Thirtieth of April
One day, Julien noticed that Mathilde was dressed completely in black. He asked a friend why.

"It's the thirtieth of April," said the friend. "Every year on this day, she wears black. It is a family story. In 1574, one of her ancestors, Boniface de La Mole, was the lover of Queen Marguerite of Navarre. He was involved in a plot against the King, and he was arrested and beheaded in Paris, on the thirtieth of April. That night, Queen Marguerite went secretly to the place of execution. She asked for his head, and she carried it away in her carriage, and buried it herself. Mademoiselle de La Mole admires that story. She thinks that it was the time of great passions, when people really lived. She wears black for him every year."
Julien was interested. "So she is not like the others," he thought.
The Ball

Some weeks later, there was a great ball at the house of the Duke de Retz. Julien went with the family. The rooms were full of light, flowers and music. Everybody was looking at Mathilde, who was the most beautiful woman at the ball.

But Mathilde was bored. She refused to dance. She watched the people around her with a cold, mocking smile. Then she noticed Julien. He was standing in a corner, talking to a foreign gentleman — Count Altamira, an Italian. Count Altamira had led a revolution in his country. It had failed, and he had been condemned to death. He had escaped to Paris, where he lived in exile.
Mathilde went closer to listen.

"Yes," Count Altamira was saying, "a death sentence. It is the only thing that cannot be bought. Everything else in our time — titles, honours, positions — everything can be bought with money. But nobody can buy a death sentence. It is the only distinction that is still real."

Julien listened with passion. Mathilde watched Julien's face, and she saw something in his eyes that she had never seen in the eyes of the young men around her: fire, energy, courage. "He is not like the others," she thought. "He is not afraid. He could be a Danton, a leader of a revolution. He could be condemned to death one day."
From that moment, she looked at Julien differently.
In the Library

In the following days, Mathilde often came to the library, where Julien was working. She asked him questions about books and history. She wanted to know what he thought. Julien answered coldly and politely. He did not like her. He thought she was proud and wanted to play with him, like a cat with a mouse.

But she continued to come. She talked to him about the past, about the great days when men fought and died for their ideas. She told him about Boniface de La Mole. Julien found that she was very intelligent, and he began to enjoy their conversations.

He also noticed that she treated him in a strange way. Sometimes she was friendly, almost warm. Sometimes she was cold and proud, as if she wanted to remind him that he was only a servant. He did not understand her.
The Young Noblemen

The young noblemen who came to the house — the Marquis de Croisenois, Count de Caylus, Count de Luz — did not like Julien. They thought he was strange, too serious and too proud. They called him "the little priest". They were polite to him, because he was the Marquis's secretary, but they did not treat him as an equal.

Mathilde compared them with Julien. "They are all so polite and so empty," she thought. "They would never do anything great or dangerous. They are afraid of everything. They only want to be admired. But Julien — he despises them, I can see it in his eyes. He is poor, but he is proud. He has a great soul. He is the only man here who is really alive."

And one day, alone in her room, Mathilde said to herself, with a kind of joy: "I love him. Yes, I love him! I, Mathilde de La Mole, am in love with my father's secretary — a carpenter's son! What a great, dangerous, extraordinary love! It is like a novel. It is worthy of Queen Marguerite!"

She did not love him the way Madame de Rênal had loved him — simply and completely, with her whole heart. She loved him with her head. She loved the idea of loving him. She loved the danger and the drama of it.

chapters.title: Part 13 — A Letter and a Trap?

paragraphs.t: Julien noticed that Mathilde was changing towards him. She looked at him more often. She came to the library almost every day. She asked his opinion in front of the young noblemen, and she listened to his answers with great attention. The young men were jealous and angry.

At first, Julien did not understand. Then he began to think. "Is it possible that she loves me? No, impossible. She is a great lady, and I am a peasant." But slowly, the idea grew in his mind. And with it grew his pride. "If she loves me," he thought, "what a victory! The proud Mathilde de La Mole, in love with the carpenter's son! What a revenge on all these nobles who look down on me!"
He did not love her. He found her proud and cold. But he wanted to win her, as he had wanted to win Madame de Rênal at Vergy — as a battle, a conquest.
The Letter
One day, a servant brought Julien a letter. It was from Mathilde. He opened it with shaking hands. It was a declaration of love.
"I need to speak to you," she wrote. "I can no longer hide what I feel. I love you."
Julien could not believe it. He read the letter again and again. Then he felt a wild joy. "I have won! I, a poor peasant, have won the love of the daughter of a marquis!"

But then a terrible suspicion came into his mind. "What if it is a trap? What if Mathilde and her brother and their friends are playing a joke on me? What if they want me to make a fool of myself, so that they can laugh at me, or even kill me? These nobles are capable of anything."

He was so afraid of a trap that he made a copy of the letter and sent the original to his friend Fouqué, far away in the mountains, to keep it safe. "If anything happens to me," he wrote to Fouqué, "publish this letter."
Then he answered Mathilde, very carefully and coldly. He did not want to show his feelings.
More Letters
Mathilde wrote again, and again. Each letter was more passionate than the last. Julien answered each one with the same careful coldness. He was waiting to see what would happen.
Then one evening, Mathilde gave him a letter in the garden. It said:
"I need to talk to you. Tonight, at one o'clock in the morning, come to my room. Take the gardener's ladder and climb up to my window. The moon will not be up."

Julien was sure that it was a trap now. "Climb up to her window at night, with a ladder, in the moonlight — in front of all the servants? If they find me, they will kill me, and say that I was a thief. Or they will laugh at me for the rest of my life."
He thought about it all day. He decided not to go. Then he thought: "If I don't go, she will think I am a coward. And I will despise myself. I must go. If it is a trap, I will die bravely."
He wrote a letter to Fouqué, telling him everything. He loaded his pistols. Then he waited.
One O'Clock

At one o'clock, Julien took the long ladder from the garden and carried it to Mathilde's window. His heart was beating fast. He looked around carefully. Nobody was there. He climbed up the ladder, with a pistol in his pocket.
The window opened. Mathilde was there.
"So you have come," she said, in a low, trembling voice. "I was not sure you would come."

She was very pale. She was as frightened as he was. Julien climbed into the room. He looked around for hidden enemies. He looked under the bed and behind the curtains. There was nobody there. It was not a trap. Mathilde really loved him.

They did not know what to say. They were both shy and nervous. Mathilde talked very fast, and very formally. She tried to be cold and proud. She said that she had decided to give herself to him because it was her duty — because he was brave and worthy, and she had promised herself. She spoke as if she were reading from a book.

At last, she gave herself to him. But it was not like Madame de Rênal. There was no tenderness, no simple joy. Both of them were acting a part. Julien was proud of his victory. Mathilde was proud of her courage. But neither of them was truly happy.
Before dawn, Julien climbed down the ladder and returned to his room.
The next morning, Julien expected Mathilde to be happy and tender. But when he saw her in the library, she was cold. She looked at him with anger in her eyes, as if she hated him.

Mathilde was ashamed. In the light of day, she regretted what she had done. "I have given myself to a man of no importance," she thought. "I, Mathilde de La Mole! I have given him a master's power over me. Now he thinks I belong to him. He will want to control me." Her pride could not bear it.
For several days, she did not speak to him. When she did, she was proud and cruel. She told him, in front of other people, that he was nothing.

Julien was in despair. He had thought that he did not love her. But now that she was rejecting him, he discovered that he did love her — passionately, madly. He could not eat, he could not sleep. He thought only of her. Her coldness made him desperate. He walked alone for hours in the garden.
The Sword
One day, they met in the library. Mathilde said to him, in a voice full of contempt:
"I am sorry I gave myself to the first person who came."

Julien felt a terrible pain. In a moment of madness, he looked around and saw an old sword hanging on the wall — a medieval sword, kept as a decoration. He took it down and pulled it out of its case. He raised it over Mathilde's head.

Mathilde did not move. She did not scream. She looked at him with shining eyes. She was not afraid; she was delighted. "He wanted to kill me!" she thought. "He is a real man, like the men of the sixteenth century! He is worthy of me!"
But Julien, seeing her look, put the sword down. He was ashamed. He hung it back on the wall and left the room.

That evening, Mathilde loved him again — more than ever. She was proud of having been loved so passionately, so dangerously. She wrote to him. That night, he climbed up the ladder to her room again, and they were happy together. She called him her master. She cut off a lock of her hair and gave it to him.
Hot and Cold

But the next day, she was cold again. And so it continued. One day she loved him, the next day she hated him. One day she was his slave, the next day she was his queen. Julien suffered terribly. He did not understand her. He only knew that he loved her and that she was torturing him.
He went to the opera and saw her there with the Marquis de Croisenois. She ignored him completely. He felt that he would die of pain.
A Secret Mission

During this time, the Marquis de La Mole gave Julien an important and secret job. One night, he took him to a house where a group of very powerful men had met — dukes, a cardinal, generals, and an important foreign minister. They were planning a political plot. They wanted foreign kings to send armies to France, to help the old nobility keep its power against the people.

Julien's job was to listen, to remember everything they said, and then to carry the message, by heart, to a powerful man in a foreign country. Nothing could be written down. The Marquis trusted Julien completely, because of his wonderful memory.

Julien listened to the conversation. He was disgusted. These men were ready to betray their own country to keep their privileges. But he did his job. He learned the whole message by heart. Then he left Paris at night and travelled by carriage across France to Strasbourg, and from there to the foreign country.
On the way, someone tried to stop him — spies, who knew that he was carrying a secret message. But Julien escaped. He delivered the message and waited for the answer.
In Strasbourg, Julien had to wait a week for the answer to his secret message. He was very unhappy. He thought only of Mathilde.

One day, in the street, he met the Russian Prince Korasoff, whom he had met in London some months before, during a trip there for the Marquis. The prince was a young, elegant, cheerful man who knew everything about love and women. He saw at once that Julien was suffering.
"My dear friend," he said, "you are in love. I can see it. And the woman is treating you badly. Tell me everything."
Julien told him the whole story, without saying Mathilde's name.

The prince laughed. "Oh, it is very simple," he said. "This young lady is proud. She loves you, but she wants to control you. As long as she knows that you love her, she will torture you. You must make her think that you do not love her any more. You must make her jealous. Choose another woman in her circle, a woman of high society, and court her. Pay her compliments. Write her love letters. Be very attentive to her — and completely cold to the young lady. You will see, she will come back to you on her knees."
"But I don't know how to write love letters," said Julien.

"Don't worry," laughed the prince. "I have a collection. Fifty-three love letters, written by a friend of mine to a very pious, very proper lady. They are perfect. You just have to copy them, one each day, and send them. Choose a lady who is religious and serious. They are the easiest to impress with these letters."
Madame de Fervaques

When Julien returned to Paris, he followed the prince's advice. He chose the Maréchale de Fervaques, a rich, beautiful widow who often came to the de La Mole house. She was very religious and very proud of her noble family. She was a little stiff and serious, and nobody had ever dared to court her.

Every evening, in the drawing room, Julien sat near Madame de Fervaques and talked to her with great attention. He told her how much he admired her virtue and her religious feelings. He did not look at Mathilde once. And every day, he copied one of the prince's letters and sent it to Madame de Fervaques.

It was very hard. The letters were long and boring, full of religious ideas and old-fashioned compliments. Sometimes Julien was so tired and unhappy that he made mistakes when he copied them. Once, he forgot to change the name of the city in the letter, and wrote "London" instead of "Paris". But Madame de Fervaques did not notice. She was flattered. Nobody had ever written such letters to her. Slowly, she began to answer them.
Mathilde's Jealousy

Mathilde watched all this. At first, she laughed at it. "He is courting that old prude? How ridiculous!" But as the weeks passed, she began to suffer. Julien never looked at her. He was always with Madame de Fervaques. He was cold and polite to her, like a stranger.
"He doesn't love me any more," she thought. "He loves that woman. I have lost him." And for the first time in her life, Mathilde de La Mole was unhappy because of a man. Her pride was broken.

One day, she found a pile of letters from Madame de Fervaques on Julien's desk, unopened. She could not stand it any longer. She went to him, pale and crying, and she fell on her knees in front of him.
"Julien," she said, "you despise me! I deserve it. But I love you. I can't live without you. I am your slave. Punish me, if you like, but don't leave me!"

Julien felt a wild joy. He had won! But he remembered the prince's advice. "If I show her how much I love her," he thought, "she will become cold and proud again. I must hide my feelings." So, although he wanted to take her in his arms, he spoke to her calmly, almost coldly.

It was the hardest thing he had ever done. But it worked. Mathilde loved him more than ever, because she was afraid of losing him. She obeyed him. She looked at him with respect and admiration. Her love became humble and passionate. Julien was happy at last — but he was always afraid. He knew that if he ever relaxed, if he ever let her see his true feelings, she would become proud and cruel again.
The News
A few months later, Mathilde told Julien a great secret. She was going to have a baby.
Julien was frightened. "Your father will kill me," he said.

But Mathilde was happy and proud. "Now we must be married," she said. "I will be your wife. I will tell my father everything. And if he refuses, I will leave his house and live with you, even in poverty."
She wrote a long letter to her father, telling him the truth.
When the Marquis de La Mole read his daughter's letter, he was furious. He called Julien to his room.
"You monster!" he shouted. "You have destroyed my family! My daughter, the daughter of the Marquis de La Mole, with a peasant — a carpenter's son! And I trusted you! I treated you like a son!"

He walked up and down, shouting and swearing. Julien stood still and said nothing. At last he said quietly: "Sir, you are right. I deserve your anger. If you want to kill me, I am ready. I will leave a letter saying that I killed myself."
The Marquis looked at him. He saw that Julien was serious. His anger became less violent, but he was still in despair.
"What can I do?" he cried. "I wanted my daughter to be a duchess! I had chosen the Marquis de Croisenois for her. And now — now everything is lost!"

For many days, the Marquis did not know what to do. He thought of sending Julien to America. He thought of sending Mathilde to a convent. He thought of fighting a duel with Julien. But Mathilde was firm.

"Father," she said, "I love Julien. I will marry him, or I will marry nobody. If you send him away, I will follow him. If you try to stop me, everyone in Paris will know the truth, and our name will be laughed at."
A New Name
At last, the Marquis decided to make the best of the situation. If his daughter must marry a nobody, he would make that nobody into a somebody.

He gave Julien some land, and a large income. He arranged for him to receive a noble title and a new name: the Chevalier Julien Sorel de La Vernaye. He even let a rumour be spread that Julien was not really the son of the carpenter, but the secret son of a nobleman. And he made him a lieutenant in a regiment of hussars — the most elegant regiment in the army.

Julien could not believe his luck. He went to Strasbourg to join his regiment. He wore a splendid uniform, red and blue, with gold decorations. He had fine horses and servants. The other officers respected him. He was a soldier at last — a lieutenant at twenty-three, almost like Napoleon's officers!

"My novel is finished," he thought proudly, "and I owe it all to myself. I have made this proud young girl love me. Her father cannot live without her, and she cannot live without me." He began to dream of becoming a colonel, and then a general.

"After all," he said to himself, "am I really the son of that carpenter? Perhaps the rumour is true. Perhaps I am the son of some great nobleman." He became proud and cold with the other officers, like a real aristocrat.
The Letter from Verrières

But the Marquis was a careful man. Before he gave his final permission for the marriage, he wanted to know more about Julien's past. He wrote to Madame de Rênal in Verrières, where Julien had been a tutor, and asked her for information about the young man's character.
Some weeks later, her answer arrived. The Marquis read it and turned pale. He showed it to Mathilde.
The letter said:

"Sir, it is my religious duty to tell you the truth, painful as it is. This young man is poor and ambitious. To succeed, he uses hypocrisy and he seduces women. When he lived in my house, he tried to win my confidence and that of my family in order to advance himself. He seduced me. He has no religion and no principles. His only aim is to make himself master of the house and of the fortune of the people he lives with. He leaves misery and regret behind him wherever he goes."

Madame de Rênal had not written this letter freely. Her confessor, a strict and jealous priest, had dictated it to her. He had told her that it was her duty to God to warn the Marquis. She had suffered terribly as she wrote it, and she had cried over every word.
The Marquis wrote immediately to Julien in Strasbourg: "I refuse to allow the marriage. I will give you money, but you must leave France at once, and never see my daughter again."
Mathilde wrote too. She sent Julien a copy of Madame de Rênal's letter. "Everything is lost," she wrote. "Come at once."
When Julien read Madame de Rênal's letter, he went pale. He did not say a word. He left the regiment at once, took a fast carriage and travelled day and night — not to Paris, but to Verrières.
It was a Sunday morning when Julien arrived in Verrières. He did not go to his father's house. He did not speak to anyone. He went straight to a gun shop.
"I want a pair of pistols," he said to the gunsmith. "Load them for me."
The gunsmith loaded them. Julien paid and put them in his pocket. Then he walked to the church.

The bells were ringing. It was the time of the morning mass. The church was full of people. Julien went in. The tall windows were covered with red curtains, just as on the day he had found the piece of newspaper, many years before. In the red light, he saw Madame de Rênal. She was kneeling at her usual place, praying.

When he saw her, his arm shook so much that at first he could not do anything. "I can't," he thought. "I can't do it." Then the bell rang for the most sacred moment of the mass, and Madame de Rênal bent her head. For a moment, under her shawl, she looked almost exactly like the woman who had loved him so much.
Julien raised his pistol and fired. He missed. He fired again. Madame de Rênal fell.
Arrest

There was a terrible noise. People screamed and ran in all directions. Julien stood still. He did not try to escape. He did not understand what he had done. When the people ran out of the church, one of them pushed him, and he fell. Someone took his pistols. Then a policeman came and arrested him.

He was taken to the prison of Verrières. They put chains on his hands. He did not resist. He did not speak. He sat on his bed and stared at the wall. "It is finished," he thought. "I have done it. I will die, and I deserve it."
He slept deeply that night, like a man who has finished a long, hard piece of work.
She Is Alive
The next day, the jailer came into his cell. "Sir," he said, "I have news. Madame de Rênal is not dead. The bullet went into her shoulder. The doctor says that she will live."
Julien jumped up. "She is not dead?" he cried. And then he fell on his knees and began to cry — great, violent tears, like a child. "She will live! Thank God! Thank God!"

At that moment, for the first time in a long time, he believed in God. He prayed. He felt that a great weight had been lifted from his heart. He did not care about himself any more. He only cared that she was alive.

He also realised something else. All his anger had disappeared. He did not hate her. He understood that the letter was not really hers — that she had written it because she was religious and afraid, and because someone had pushed her to do it. And he understood that she was the only woman he had ever really loved.
Prison
Some days later, Julien was taken to Besançon, to the big prison in the old castle. He was given a room high up in a tower. From his window, he had a beautiful view of the city and the mountains.
He was calm, almost happy. He spent his days reading and thinking. He did not want to be saved. "I have tried to kill a woman," he said. "I deserve to die. Let them judge me."

The jailer was very kind to him. Julien soon discovered why: someone was sending him money every day to treat the young prisoner well. It was Madame de Rênal. She was not angry with him at all. She was secretly happy that he had tried to kill her, because it meant that he still loved her. As soon as she could get out of bed, she wrote to the jury members, and to the judges, and to the priests, begging them to save his life.
"If he dies," she thought, "I will die too."
But she did not visit him. Her husband would not allow it. And her confessor told her that it would be a terrible sin.

When Mathilde heard the news, she left Paris at once, without telling her father. She came to Besançon in disguise, wearing simple clothes and a big hat, under a false name. She bribed the jailers and came to see Julien in his prison.
