She threw herself into his arms. "Julien!" she cried. "I am here! I will save you! I will do everything — everything!"
Julien was moved by her courage. She had left her family, her reputation, her comfortable life, to come to him. She was like Queen Marguerite, who had risked everything for Boniface de La Mole.

Mathilde was excited. She thought her situation was very romantic. She worked day and night to save him. She went to see the judges, the lawyers, and the important people of Besançon. She spent a lot of money. She even went to see a powerful priest, Father de Frilair, who controlled many people in the city. He promised to help — if she could get a favour for him from her family in Paris.
"I will get you out of here," she said to Julien every day. "We will escape to America, or to Italy. We will be free."
Julien's Thoughts

But Julien was tired of her heroism. She talked so much, she was so excited, she was always acting a part. He admired her, but he did not love her. Every day, he thought more and more of Madame de Rênal — of her gentle face, her simple love, the happy days at Vergy, the lime tree in the garden, the walks in the woods.
"Mathilde loves me with her head," he thought. "She loves the drama of my situation. But Madame de Rênal loved me with her heart. She loved me for myself. And I have tried to kill her."

He began to see his life clearly, perhaps for the first time. He had been so busy with his ambition, so busy pretending and calculating, that he had never really lived. He had chased power and success, and he had not seen the happiness that was right in front of him.
"I was happy at Vergy," he said to himself, "and I did not know it. Ambition carried me away to imaginary lands. Now that I am going to die, I understand."
Fouqué
His friend Fouqué came to see him too. Fouqué was a simple man, but he had a big heart. He wanted to sell everything he owned to bribe the jailers and help Julien escape. Julien was moved to tears.
"No, my friend," he said. "Keep your money. I don't want to escape. But thank you. You are the only true friend I have ever had."
Death
Julien thought a lot about death. He was not afraid of it. He had always admired brave men who died for their ideas, like Count Altamira, or like Boniface de La Mole. Now he would die too.

"What is death?" he said to himself. "Napoleon died on a small island in the middle of the ocean. Danton died on the guillotine. Every great man dies. It is not death that matters, but how one dies. I will die calmly, without fear, like a soldier."
He looked out of his window at the beautiful sky, and at the mountains, and he felt strangely peaceful.
The date of the trial came closer.

The day of the trial arrived. The whole region was talking about it. A young, handsome man, a former seminary student, had tried to kill the wife of the mayor of Verrières, in a church, during mass! It was like a novel. People came from all over to see the trial. The courtroom was full. Many fine ladies were there, dressed in their best clothes, and many of them cried when they saw the young prisoner.
Julien was brought in by two policemen. He was pale but calm, and very elegant in his black clothes. When the ladies saw how young and handsome he was, they whispered with pity.

Mathilde had done everything possible to save him. She had bribed many people. Father de Frilair had promised her that the jury would be kind to Julien. But there was one problem: the foreman of the jury — the man who would lead the jury and announce the verdict — was Monsieur Valenod. He had become very important and rich. He was now the new mayor of Verrières. And he hated Julien.

The lawyer for the prosecution spoke for a long time. He said that Julien was a dangerous young man, ambitious and immoral, who had seduced his employer's wife and then tried to kill her. The lawyer for the defence spoke too. He said that Julien had acted in a moment of madness, and that the jury should have mercy on him.
Julien's Speech
Then the judge asked Julien if he wished to say anything. Julien stood up. The courtroom was silent.

"Gentlemen of the jury," he said, in a clear, calm voice. "I do not ask for your mercy. I am not deceiving myself. I deserve death. I tried to kill the most worthy woman in the world, a woman who had been like a mother to me. My crime was horrible, and it was planned. I deserve to die.

"But even if I were less guilty, I see men here who would want to punish me anyway. They do not care about my crime. They care about who I am. I see in front of me men who want to punish, in me, a class of young men — young men born poor, in a humble class, who have had the good luck to get an education, and who have dared to mix with what the rich call 'good society'.

"That is my real crime, gentlemen. And it will be punished more severely because I am not being judged by my equals. I do not see any rich peasants on this jury. I see only rich men who are angry that a carpenter's son has dared to rise above his class."
The courtroom was in an uproar. The ladies cried. Some men were angry. Monsieur Valenod went red.
Julien sat down. He had spoken for twenty minutes. He knew that his words had destroyed any hope of mercy. But he had said the truth, and he was proud of it.
The Verdict
The jury left the room to decide. It was late in the evening. The people waited, whispering. Hours passed. At last, at about one o'clock in the morning, the jury came back.
Monsieur Valenod stood up, very seriously, and read the verdict. Julien was guilty of attempted murder, with planning. The judge then announced the sentence: death.
Julien looked at Valenod and smiled. "Well," he thought, "Valenod has his revenge. Now he will marry Madame de Rênal when her husband dies. He has wanted her for years. How he must be enjoying this!"
In the courtroom, many women were crying. Mathilde, hidden among the crowd, fainted.
Madame de Rênal was not there. She had been too ill to come. When she heard the verdict, she fell to the floor, and for a long time she could not speak.

After the trial, Julien was put in a cell for prisoners condemned to death. It was small and dark, and it smelled bad. Mathilde came every day. She wanted him to ask for an appeal — to ask a higher court to change the sentence. "There is still hope," she said. "My father has powerful friends. If you appeal, we can save you."
But Julien refused. "I am ready to die," he said. "Why should I live? To be a prisoner for the rest of my life? No. Let me die."
Mathilde cried and begged, but he did not change his mind.
She Comes
Then one day, the door of his cell opened, and Madame de Rênal came in.
She had escaped from her husband's house. She had come alone to Besançon. She ran to Julien and threw herself into his arms, crying.

"Julien! Julien!" she said. "Forgive me! Forgive me for that terrible letter! It was not me who wrote it. My confessor told me what to write. He said that it was my duty to God. I wrote it, and I have hated myself every day since then."
Julien held her in his arms. He kissed her hands and her face. He cried too. "It is you who must forgive me," he said. "I tried to kill you. I was mad."
"I forgave you the moment the bullet hit me," she said. "When I knew it was you, I was happy. It meant that you still loved me."

They sat together for a long time, holding each other's hands, like two children. They talked about Vergy, about the lime tree, about the butterflies, about the first evening when he held her hand. They laughed and cried at the same time.
"I never loved anyone but you," said Julien. "In Paris, I was mad with ambition. I wanted to be great. But I only had one real moment of happiness in my life, and that was with you."

She promised to come every day. And she did. She bribed the jailers to let her in. For a few weeks, Julien was happier than he had ever been in his life. He forgot about death. He forgot about Paris and Mathilde and ambition. He only thought about her.
"Before you came," he said to her, "I thought that I was strong and ready to die. Now I am happy, and that makes death harder. But I am not afraid."

He asked her to make him one promise. "Promise me that you will not kill yourself when I die. Promise me that you will live, and look after your children, and also after my child — the child that Mathilde is going to have. They will need you."
She promised.
Visitors
Madame de Rênal's husband found out where she was, and he ordered her to come home. She had to obey. But before she left, she held Julien in her arms for a long time.

Julien's father also came to see him. The old man did not come to comfort his son. He came to talk about money. Julien understood, and he gave him all the money he had. The old peasant was satisfied, and he left. "A father who loves money," thought Julien, "and a son who loved glory. We are not so different after all."
Mathilde came too, but Julien was tired of her. She was jealous of Madame de Rênal, and she made scenes. He was polite to her, but his heart was far away.
The End

On the morning of the execution, the sun was shining. It was a beautiful day. Julien walked out of the prison calmly, with his head high. He felt brave and strong. He thought of the walks in the woods at Vergy, of the beautiful mountains, of the fresh air. "Everything happened simply," Stendhal writes, "and without any affectation on his part." He did not make speeches. He did not show fear. He walked to the guillotine like a man walking in a garden.
And it was over.
Afterwards
Fouqué had bought Julien's body. That night, he sat alone in his room, beside it, crying. Then the door opened, and Mathilde came in. She was dressed in black, and her face was pale and wild.
"I want to see him," she said.

Fouqué could not refuse. She took Julien's head in her hands and kissed his forehead. She was thinking of Queen Marguerite, who had done the same thing for Boniface de La Mole, three hundred years before.

Julien had once said to Fouqué that he wanted to be buried in the little cave in the mountains above Verrières, where he had gone as a boy to be alone and to dream. Fouqué and Mathilde took his body there, at night, in a carriage. Many priests followed, singing. In the light of many candles, Mathilde, alone in her carriage, carried on her knees the head of the man she had loved so much. When they arrived, she buried it with her own hands. Then she had the cave decorated with Italian marble, at great expense.
Madame de Rênal kept her promise. She did not try to kill herself. But three days after Julien's death, she died, holding her children in her arms.

grammar.title: Verb to be (present)
grammar.form: I am · you/we/they are · he/she/it is. Negativa: is not (isn't), are not (aren't). Pergunta: Is he...? Are you...?
grammar.explanation: O verbo to be significa ser ou estar. É o verbo mais comum do inglês. Ele aparece sozinho, antes de adjetivos (She is tired), de substantivos (He is a captain) e de lugares (They are in the ship).

grammar.title: Present simple
grammar.form: I/you/we/they work · he/she/it works. Negativa: don't / doesn't + verbo. Pergunta: Do you...? Does he...?
grammar.explanation: Usado para hábitos, rotinas, fatos e verdades gerais: The sun rises in the east. Atenção ao -s na terceira pessoa do singular (he lives, she goes, it has). Nos livros, aparece muito em diálogos e em explicações do narrador.

grammar.title: There is / there are
grammar.form: There is + singular · There are + plural. Passado: there was / there were.
grammar.explanation: Equivale a 'há' ou 'existe' em português. Use there is para uma coisa e there are para várias: There are three boats. No passado: There was a strange light.

grammar.title: Present continuous
grammar.form: am / is / are + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Para ações que estão acontecendo agora ou neste período: The ship is sinking! Também é usado para planos já combinados para o futuro: We are leaving tomorrow.

grammar.title: Imperative
grammar.form: Verbo na forma básica: Come! Look! Negativo: Don't + verbo: Don't go!
grammar.explanation: Para dar ordens, conselhos e instruções. Não há sujeito: Stand up! Lower the boats! Para ser mais educado, acrescente please.

grammar.title: Can / could (ability and permission)
grammar.form: can / could + verbo básico. Negativa: cannot (can't), could not (couldn't).
grammar.explanation: Can expressa capacidade ou permissão no presente: I can swim. Could é o passado de can (He could not move) e também uma forma educada de pedir (Could you help me?).

grammar.title: Verb to be (past)
grammar.form: I/he/she/it was · you/we/they were. Negativa: wasn't / weren't.
grammar.explanation: O passado de to be: was e were. The night was cold. They were afraid. É uma das formas mais frequentes em narrativas.

grammar.title: Past simple (regular verbs)
grammar.form: verbo + -ed: walk → walked, arrive → arrived, stop → stopped. Negativa e pergunta: did not (didn't) / Did...? + verbo básico.
grammar.explanation: Para ações terminadas no passado. É o tempo principal das histórias: He opened the door and looked inside. Os verbos regulares formam o passado com -ed.

grammar.title: Past simple (irregular verbs)
grammar.form: formas próprias: go → went, see → saw, take → took, come → came, say → said...
grammar.explanation: Muitos verbos comuns não usam -ed no passado e precisam ser memorizados. Ler muito é a melhor forma de fixá-los: The whale rose out of the water. She saw him in the church.

grammar.title: Past continuous
grammar.form: was / were + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Para uma ação que estava em andamento no passado, muitas vezes interrompida por outra: I was writing when the Count came in. Também descreve o cenário de uma cena: The wind was blowing and the waves were rising.

grammar.title: Going to (future)
grammar.form: am / is / are going to + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Para intenções e planos (I am going to meet a nobleman) e para previsões baseadas no que vemos (The ship is going to sink!). No passado, was going to indica um plano que talvez não aconteceu.

grammar.title: Will (future)
grammar.form: will ('ll) + verbo básico. Negativa: will not (won't).
grammar.explanation: Para decisões no momento da fala, promessas e previsões: I will come back. He won't escape. Em textos antigos aparece também shall, com sentido parecido (I shall wait).

grammar.title: Comparatives and superlatives
grammar.form: Curtos: -er / the -est (big, bigger, the biggest). Longos: more / the most (more beautiful, the most beautiful). Irregulares: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst.
grammar.explanation: Para comparar duas coisas (The sperm whale is bigger than the right whale) ou destacar uma entre todas (the largest animal in the world).

grammar.title: Present perfect
grammar.form: have / has + particípio passado (seen, done, written, arrived)
grammar.explanation: Liga o passado ao presente: experiências de vida (I have never seen such a whale), ações recentes com resultado agora (He has lost his leg) e situações que começaram no passado e continuam (I have lived here for fifty years). Não se usa com tempo passado definido (yesterday, in 1820).

grammar.title: Must / have to (obligation)
grammar.form: must + verbo básico · have to / has to / had to + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Must expressa obrigação ou necessidade forte, muitas vezes vinda de quem fala: I must go. Have to expressa obrigação externa e é usado em todos os tempos: We had to wait. Mustn't significa proibição; don't have to significa que não é necessário.

grammar.title: Should / ought to (advice)
grammar.form: should + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Para conselhos, opiniões e o que é correto fazer: You should rest. A man should keep his warmth inside him. Equivale a 'deveria'.

grammar.title: First conditional
grammar.form: If + presente simples, will + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Para condições reais ou prováveis no futuro: If you go, I will follow you. If he finds it, I am lost. A oração com if pode vir antes ou depois.

grammar.title: Verb + to-infinitive / -ing
grammar.form: want/decide/try/begin/hope + to + verbo · enjoy/stop/finish/keep/like + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Alguns verbos são seguidos de to + verbo (He decided to go), outros de verbo-ing (She stopped crying). Alguns aceitam os dois, às vezes com sentidos diferentes (stop to talk = parar para conversar; stop talking = parar de conversar).

grammar.title: Passive voice
grammar.form: be (no tempo desejado) + particípio passado: is made, was killed, has been seen, will be found
grammar.explanation: Usada quando a ação é mais importante do que quem a pratica, ou quando não sabemos quem a praticou: The boat was broken in half. The ship was named after a tribe. Para dizer quem fez, use by: He was killed by a whale.

grammar.title: Past perfect
grammar.form: had + particípio passado
grammar.explanation: Para uma ação que aconteceu antes de outra ação no passado: When we arrived, the ship had already left. Equivale ao 'tinha feito' do português. É muito comum em narrativas, para voltar no tempo.

grammar.title: Relative clauses
grammar.form: who (pessoas) · which (coisas) · that (pessoas ou coisas) · whose (posse) · where (lugar)
grammar.explanation: Dão informação sobre um substantivo: the man who sold heads; the boat which was broken; the woman whose son was lost. Who e that podem ser omitidos quando são objeto: the book (that) I read.

grammar.title: Reported speech
grammar.form: say / tell + (that) + oração, normalmente com o tempo verbal recuado: 'I am ill' → He said that he was ill.
grammar.explanation: Para contar o que alguém disse sem usar aspas. Os tempos costumam recuar um passo no passado (am → was, will → would, have seen → had seen). Use tell + pessoa (He told me...) e say sem pessoa (He said...).

grammar.title: Second conditional
grammar.form: If + passado simples, would + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Para situações imaginárias ou improváveis no presente ou no futuro: If I had a gun, I would destroy him. Com o verbo to be, a forma formal é were para todas as pessoas: If I were you...

grammar.title: Present perfect continuous
grammar.form: have / has been + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Para uma ação que começou no passado e continua até agora, com ênfase na duração: I have been waiting for hours. I have been thinking about it.

grammar.title: Past perfect continuous
grammar.form: had been + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Para uma ação que estava em andamento até um momento do passado: She had been crying when he arrived. Mostra duração antes de outro acontecimento passado.

grammar.title: Modals of deduction
grammar.form: must / might / may / could / can't + be ou + verbo
grammar.explanation: Para expressar certeza ou possibilidade sobre algo que deduzimos: It must be the Count (tenho quase certeza). He might be asleep (talvez). It can't be true (não é possível).

grammar.title: Third conditional
grammar.form: If + had + particípio, would have + particípio
grammar.explanation: Para imaginar um passado diferente do que aconteceu: If I had listened to him, none of this would have happened. Expressa arrependimento ou consequências que não aconteceram.

grammar.title: Phrasal verbs
grammar.form: verbo + partícula (up, down, out, off, on, in, back...)
grammar.explanation: Verbos combinados com uma partícula que muitas vezes muda o sentido: give up (desistir), find out (descobrir), wake up (acordar). Os mais comuns dos livros também aparecem na aba Vocabulário, em Expressões.
